title: The Odyssey Review: Nolan's Greek Epic Is a Spectacle Worth the Voyage — Mostly
excerpt: Christopher Nolan's $250 million IMAX adaptation of Homer earns its epic ambitions with a stunning score and strong ensemble, even if some island adventures test your patience.
body:
By Editor

  • Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey is a sweeping, nearly three-hour adaptation of Homer's epic poem, shot entirely on IMAX 70mm cameras across seven countries with a $250 million budget.
  • Ludwig Göransson's score is the film's standout — a pulse-pounding soundscape that elevates every sequence, even on a regular screen.
  • The film excels at drawing newcomers into Greek mythology, making audiences curious about characters and stories they may never have encountered.
  • Some island adventures drag, and the pacing dips in stretches where spectacle alone can't sustain momentum — but these are minor blemishes on an otherwise grand achievement.

Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey is the kind of movie Hollywood rarely makes anymore — a sprawling, R-rated epic adapted from one of the oldest stories in human history, asking audiences to sit with mythology rather than rush through it. Two weeks into its theatrical run, it has already grossed over $720 million worldwide, opened to $264 million globally (Nolan's biggest debut ever), and become the largest live-action opening of 2026. The numbers say blockbuster. The film itself says something more interesting.

Matt Damon leads as Odysseus, the king of Ithaca who spends a decade fighting the Trojan War and another decade trying to get home — thwarted by gods, monsters, and his own hubris. Anne Hathaway plays Penelope, his wife left behind to fend off a court full of entitled suitors while raising their son Telemachus (Tom Holland) alone. Nolan, adapting the script himself, draws from Homer's Odyssey, Virgil's Aeneid, and other classical sources to build something that feels both faithful to the ancient material and distinctly his own.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mzw2ttJD2qQ

A Gateway Into Myth

What The Odyssey does best is make you genuinely curious. If you're not steeped in Greek mythology, the film doesn't hold your hand, but it doesn't leave you behind either. You'll find yourself wondering why Penelope's household is under siege the way it is, what drives the strange encounters on each island — the Cyclops Polyphemus, the witch Circe, the nymph Calypso — and why these mythic figures behave the way they do.

https://x.com/EricBalchunas/status/2083349736732475726

Nolan trusts the audience to sit in that curiosity, and it pays off. The Trojan Horse sequence alone, reimagined as a half-buried metal figure rising from a beach rather than the standard upright wooden toy, sets the tone: this isn't the mythology you grew up with in textbooks. As Roger Ebert's Matt Zoller Seitz noted in his review, "You may expect to see again what so many other filmmakers have shown you, and instead are presented with a new take on an old tale."

"There's plenty to see here. Some of it will leave folks wondering, 'Hold on, did I forget about that part?'"

The Score Is the Highlight

If there's one element that elevates every frame of The Odyssey, it's Ludwig Göransson's score. Coming off his Oscar-winning work on Oppenheimer, Göransson delivers something that might be even better here. The music doesn't just accompany the visuals — it pulls you into the world. Sea crossings feel vast, battles feel chaotic but controlled, and the quieter moments in Ithaca carry real emotional weight.

Even watching on a regular screen — not IMAX — the background score was the standout of the entire experience. It's the kind of music that stays with you walking out of the theater, humming something you can't quite name. Battles use creaking wood, crashing waves, and long pockets of silence to build dread before the score comes crashing back. Don't be surprised if this earns Göransson back-to-back Academy Awards.

Performances That Hold

The ensemble is uniformly strong. Damon carries the film with a performance that shifts convincingly between warrior, king, trickster, and broken man — a character who pontificates about honor but violates his own code when it suits him. Hathaway brings real fire to Penelope; this isn't a passive wife waiting at home but a woman seething at the entitlement stripping her household bare. Holland gives Telemachus a searching quality, a young man trying to figure out who he is in the shadow of a father he's never known. When Damon and Holland finally share the screen, those scenes land among the film's most moving.

Robert Pattinson as the slimy suitor Antinous is the kind of villain you want to reach through the screen and slap — all oily charm and punchable conviction. Samantha Morton's Circe is unsettling in the best way, her eerie stillness making the island sequence genuinely horrifying. Zendaya's Athena, while excellent, doesn't get much screen time — she mostly stares judgmentally at Odysseus from a distance only he can see. And John Leguizamo as the blind servant Eumaeus, speaking in his natural Bronx accent, is a quiet reminder that Nolan's casting choices are deliberate and inclusive.

Where It Drags

At 173 minutes, The Odyssey earns most of its runtime, but not all of it. Some of the island adventures feel slow — episodes that work as self-contained chapters in Homer's poem but lose momentum when strung together on screen. The pacing dips during certain mythological detours where the spectacle alone isn't enough to carry the weight. Nolan's non-linear storytelling, shuffling between distant past, recent past, and present, is mostly effective but occasionally makes an already dense narrative harder to follow than it needs to be.

These lulls don't sink the film. They're brief dips in an otherwise steady voyage. But in a nearly three-hour movie, they're noticeable.

Visually Consistent, Built to Last

The film looks remarkable. Shot entirely on IMAX 70mm across Morocco, Greece, Italy, Scotland, Iceland, Western Sahara, and Malta, Hoyte van Hoytema's cinematography gives the film a tactile, physical quality that CGI-heavy blockbusters can't match. You can almost feel the weight of the Trojan Horse being dragged on rolling logs, the heat of a collapsing building, the salt spray at sea. Nolan's commitment to practical effects — the first feature film shot entirely on IMAX — keeps the whole film grounded even when gods and sea monsters are on screen.

The visual consistency is impressive throughout. Nolan maintains a cohesive look and tone across wildly different settings — from the sun-bleached beaches of Troy to the dark waters of Odysseus's sea crossings to the political tension of Ithaca's court — without any of it feeling disjointed.

The Verdict

The Odyssey isn't Nolan's tightest film — Oppenheimer had sharper focus, The Dark Knight had leaner pacing. But it might be his most ambitious, and it largely delivers on that ambition. It's a film that sends you home wanting to read Homer, wondering about the stories behind the stories, and humming a score you can't shake.

For the uninitiated, it's an invitation into mythology. For everyone else, it's proof that Hollywood can still build something epic, earnest, and made for the biggest screen you can find.

Rating: ★★★★ (4/5)

The Odyssey is in theaters now. Directed by Christopher Nolan. Starring Matt Damon, Anne Hathaway, Tom Holland, Robert Pattinson, Zendaya, Lupita Nyong'o, Samantha Morton, Charlize Theron, and John Leguizamo. Rated R. Runtime: 173 minutes.
